      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> is a hollow tube that carries food and liquids from your throat to your stomach.  Early <span class="qt0">esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> usually does not cause symptoms. Later, you may have symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Painful or difficult swallowing</li><li>Weight loss</li><li>A hoarse voice or cough that doesn't go away</li></ul><p>You're at greater risk for getting <span class="qt0">esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> if you smoke, drink heavily, or have acid reflux. Your risk also goes up as you age</p><p> Your doctor uses imaging tests and a biopsy to diagnose <span class="qt0">esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.  Treatments include surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.  You might also need nutritional support, since the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or treatment may make it hard to swallow.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/esophagusdisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Esophagus</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Achalasia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Barrett's <span class="qt0">Esophagus</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiospasm</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders?<p><span class="qt0">Esophagus</span> disorders are problems with how your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> works. The <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> is the tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach. You usually don't notice it unless you swallow something too big, hot, or cold. You might also notice it if something is wrong. When that happens, you might feel pain or have trouble swallowing (dysphagia).</p>What causes <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders?<p>The cause depends on the type of disorder. Some run in families. Others are linked to allergic reactions to food or substances in your environment. Sometimes, the cause is unknown.</p><p>You may be more likely to develop an <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorder if you:</p><ul><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are pregnant</li><li>Take certain medicines</li><li>Have had radiation treatmentt to your neck or chest</li><li>Smoke or are around secondhand smoke</li></ul>What are common <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders?<p>The most common <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> problem is gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). This happens when the muscle at the bottom of your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> doesn't close properly. Stomach acid can move back up and irritate the <span class="qt0">esophagus</span>.</p><p>Other <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders include:</p><ul><li>Heartburn is a burning feeling in your chest or throat. It is often caused by acid reflux.</li><li>Barrett's <span class="qt0">Esophagus</span> happens when the lining of your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> changes. It is often caused by chronic (long-term) GERD.</li><li>Achalasia is a problem where the lower muscle in your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> doesn't relax like it should.</li><li><span class="qt0">Esophageal</span> Spasms are muscle contractions that cause chest pain or swallowing problems.</li><li>Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE) is a rare condition where certain white blood cells (eosinophils) build up in the <span class="qt0">esophagus</span>, causing swelling, pain, and trouble swallowing.</li><li><span class="qt0">Esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> is a type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that starts in the tissues of the <span class="qt0">esophagus</span>.</li></ul>What are symptoms of <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders?<p>Symptoms can be different for each condition but may include:</p><ul><li>Pain in your chest, abdomen (belly), or back</li><li>A cough or sore throat that doesn't go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing or feeling like food is stuck</li><li>A hoarse voice or wheezing</li><li>Heartburn or a burning feeling in your stomach</li><li>Tasting acid or food in the back of your mouth</li><li>Food or liquid coming back up into your mouth (regurgitation)</li><li>Losing weight without trying</li></ul><p>Get medical help right away if you have chest pain with shortness of breath, or pain in your jaw or arm. These could be signs of a heart problem.</p>How are <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. They may order one or more tests, such as:</p><ul><li>Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy. This test uses a tiny camera to look inside your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> and stomach.</li><li>Biopsy. This test takes a small tissue sample to check.</li><li>Barium swallow. This test uses imaging to see how you swallow.</li><li><span class="qt0">Esophageal</span> manometry. This test checks how well your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> moves food to your stomach.</li><li><span class="qt0">Esophageal</span> pH test. This test measures how often acid backs up into your <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> and how long the acid stays there.</li></ul>How are <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders treated?<p>Treatment depends on what's causing the problem and your overall health. Some <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders get better with over-the-counter medicines, diet changes, or lifestyle changes. Others may need prescription medicine or surgery.</p><p>Without treatment, some disorders may lead to other problems, such as pneumonia, from food entering the windpipe. GERD, Barrett's <span class="qt0">esophagus</span>, and achalasia can also raise your risk for <span class="qt0">esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>Can <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> disorders be prevented?<p>You can help prevent or reduce symptoms by:</p><ul><li>Not smoking and limiting alcohol</li><li>Eating smaller meals</li><li>Avoiding eating close to bedtime</li><li>Wearing loose-fitting clothes</li><li>Sleeping on your left side or raising the head of your bed</li><li>Maintaining a healthy weight</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/headandneckcancer.html">
      <content name="title">Head and Neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>? <p>Head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is the name for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> are squamous cell <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>. They begin in the moist tissues that line the head and neck. The <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> grows.</p><p>There are other <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> that develop in the head and neck, such as brain <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, eye <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, and <span class="qt0">esophageal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. But they are usually not considered to be head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>, because those types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>? <p>Anyone can get head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of head or neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Have HPV (for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the head and neck (for salivary gland <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The symptoms of head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>A lump in the neck</li><li>A sore in the mouth or the throat that does not heal and may be painful</li><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>How is head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the area that might have <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The treatment for head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> will depend on the specific type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, the stage (how advanced the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells and cause less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent head and neck <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/benefitsofexercise.html">
      <content name="title">Benefits of Exercise</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Exercise Benefits</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>We have heard it many times before -- regular exercise is good for you, and it can help you manage your weight. But if you are like many people, you are busy, you sit most of the day at your job, and you haven't yet changed your exercise habits. The good news is that it's never too late to start. You can start slowly and find ways to fit more physical activity into your life. To get the most benefit, you should try to get the recommended amount of physical activity for your age. If you can do that, the payoff is that you will feel better, may help prevent or control many diseases, and will likely even live longer.</p>What are the health benefits of exercise?<p>Regular exercise and physical activity may:</p><ul><li>Help you get to and stay at a healthy weight. Along with diet, exercise plays an important role in maintaining a healthy weight and preventing obesity. If you are at a healthy weight, you can maintain it if the calories you eat and drink are equal to the amount of energy you burn. To lose weight, you need to use more calories than you eat and drink.</li><li>Reduce your risk of heart diseases. Exercise strengthens your heart and improves your circulation. The increased blood flow raises the oxygen levels in your body. This helps lower your risk of heart diseases such as coronary artery disease and heart attack. Regular exercise can also lower high blood pressure, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels, all of which are risk factors for heart disease.</li><li>Help your body manage blood glucose (blood sugar) and insulin levels. Exercise can lower your blood glucose levels and help your insulin work better. This can reduce your risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. And if you already have one of these diseases, exercise can help you manage it.</li><li>Help you manage a chronic health condition. For example, regular physical activity may help reduce pain and improve function in adults with arthritis. It can also help support daily living activities for people with disabilities. This may help them be more independent.</li><li>Help you quit smoking. Exercise may make it easier to quit smoking by reducing your cravings and withdrawal symptoms. It can also help limit the weight you might gain when you stop smoking.</li><li>Improve your mental health and mood. During exercise, your body releases chemicals that can improve your mood and make you feel more relaxed. This can help you deal with stress, manage anxiety, and reduce your risk of depression.</li><li>Help keep your thinking, learning, and judgment skills sharp as you age. Exercise stimulates your body to release proteins and other chemicals that improve the structure and function of your brain.</li><li>Strengthen your bones and muscles. Regular exercise can help kids and teens build strong bones. Later in life, it can also slow the loss of bone density that comes with age. Doing muscle-strengthening activities can help you increase or maintain your muscle mass and strength. For older adults, this can mean staying independent, like being able to get in and out of a chair or bed without help.</li><li>Reduce your risk of some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>, including colon, breast, uterine, bladder, <span class="qt0">esophageal</span>, kidney, stomach, and lung <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. There are different ways that physical activity may lower the risk of these <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>. For example, it can strengthen your immune system and reduce inflammation in your body. It also helps prevent obesity, which is a risk factor for many <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</li><li>Reduce your risk of falls. For older adults, doing balance and muscle-strengthening activities can help reduce your risk of falling.</li><li>Improve your sleep. Exercise can help you fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer.</li><li>Boost your energy. Exercise helps your heart and lungs work better, which can leave you feeling more energetic throughout the day.</li><li>Improve your sexual health. Regular exercise may lower the risk of erectile dysfunction (ED) in men. For those who already have ED, exercise may help improve their sexual function. In women, exercise may increase sexual arousal.</li><li>Increase your chances of living longer. Studies show that physical activity can reduce your risk of dying early from the leading causes of death, like heart disease and certain <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</li></ul>How can I make exercise a part of my regular routine?<p>Here are some tips to help you make exercise part of your daily routine:</p><ul><li>Make everyday activities more active. Even small changes can help. You can take the stairs instead of the elevator. Walk down the hall to a coworker's office instead of sending an email. Wash the car yourself. Park further away from your destination.</li><li>Be active with friends and family. Having a workout partner may make you more likely to enjoy exercise. You can also plan social activities that involve exercise. Consider joining an exercise group or class, such as a dance class, hiking club, or volleyball team.</li><li>Keep track of your progress. Keeping a log of your activity or using a fitness tracker may help you set goals and stay motivated.</li><li>Make exercise more fun. Try listening to music or watching TV while you exercise. Also, mix things up a little bit - if you stick with just one type of exercise, you might get bored. Try doing a combination of activities.</li><li>Find activities that you can do even when the weather is bad. You can walk in a mall, climb stairs, or work out in a gym even if the weather stops you from exercising outside.</li><li>Remember that some physical activity is better than none.  Do what you can! Even 5 minutes of physical activity has real health benefits.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/cirrhosis.html">
      <content name="title">Cirrhosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Liver Cirrhosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hepatic fibrosis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Cirrhosis is scarring of the liver. Scar tissue forms because of injury or long-term disease. Scar tissue cannot do what healthy liver tissue does - make protein, help fight infections, clean the blood, help digest food and store energy.   Cirrhosis can lead to  :</p><ul><li>Easy bruising or bleeding, or nosebleeds</li><li>Swelling of the abdomen or legs </li><li>Extra sensitivity to medicines</li><li>High blood pressure in the vein entering the liver</li><li>Enlarged veins called varices in the <span class="qt0">esophagus</span> and stomach. Varices can bleed suddenly.</li><li> Kidney failure</li><li>Jaundice</li><li>Severe itching</li><li>Gallstones</li></ul><p>A small number of people with cirrhosis get liver <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Your doctor will diagnose cirrhosis with blood tests, imaging tests, or a biopsy.</p><p>Cirrhosis has many causes. In the United States, the most common causes are chronic alcoholism and hepatitis. Nothing will make the scar tissue disappear, but treating the cause can keep it from getting worse. If too much scar tissue forms, you may need to consider a liver transplant.  </p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
